paragraphs: This paper studies how a system can learn physical behavior from few observations, including situations where some properties are hidden. Its Bayesian-symbolic framework, BSP, represents an environment as interacting entities governed by unknown force laws. The model treats entity properties as random variables, allowing it to represent uncertainty while reasoning about what it observes.

BSP combines two learning tasks. Bayesian inference estimates unknown properties of the entities, while symbolic regression searches for force laws expressed through a grammar of Newtonian physics. An iterative expectation-maximization procedure connects these tasks: estimates of properties inform the search for laws, and learned laws inform subsequent estimates. This lets the system learn physical relationships while retaining uncertainty about the underlying entities.

On controlled synthetic datasets, BSP is more sample-efficient than the neural alternatives evaluated. The authors also demonstrate applications to real-world common-sense scenes and examine tasks used to study human physical reasoning. Their findings support combining explicit physical structure with uncertainty-aware inference for learning from limited observations.
neurips-2021-a-bayesian-symbolic-approac.tldr: BSP combines Bayesian inference and symbolic force-law discovery to learn physical behavior efficiently from limited observations.

paragraphs: Video object segmentation requires identifying which image regions belong to each target as a video progresses. In multi-object scenes, methods that handle one target at a time repeat matching and segmentation work. This paper introduces Associating Objects with Transformers, or AOT, to process several targets together within a shared representation.

An identification mechanism associates multiple targets with the same high-dimensional embedding space while preserving their identities. Matching objects and decoding their segmentation can then happen jointly. A Long Short-Term Transformer builds hierarchical matching and propagation, providing the machinery for maintaining these associations across the video. The approach addresses both how objects are represented and how their identities are carried forward.

Experiments cover single-object and multi-object benchmarks and several model sizes. The larger R50-AOT-L variant outperforms the compared methods on YouTube-VOS and both DAVIS benchmarks while delivering more than three times faster multi-object runtime. The smaller AOT-T maintains real-time multi-object speed. These findings show that shared object association can improve accuracy and computational efficiency together.
neurips-2021-associating-objects-with-tr.tldr: AOT jointly matches and segments multiple video objects through shared embeddings and a Transformer, improving accuracy and runtime in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Equivariant neural networks encode how their outputs should change when their inputs undergo a symmetry transformation. Existing approaches typically require knowing the symmetry group beforehand and discretizing continuous groups. This paper introduces the Lie algebra convolutional network, L-conv, which works with infinitesimal generators: descriptions of the small transformations underlying a continuous symmetry.

Using this representation, L-conv can discover symmetries automatically without discretizing the group. The authors show that it can serve as a building block for any group-equivariant feedforward architecture. They also express convolutional neural networks and graph convolutional networks as instances of L-conv with suitable groups. This provides a common framework for architectures whose structural assumptions otherwise appear different.

The paper additionally establishes connections to physics. Group-invariant losses generalize field theory, an Euler-Lagrange equation measures robustness, and equivariance leads to conservation laws and a Noether current. These connections offer theoretical directions for designing broader families of equivariant networks and applying them to physical science problems.
neurips-2021-automatic-symmetry-discover.tldr: L-conv uses infinitesimal symmetry generators to discover symmetries automatically and connect equivariant network design with physical principles.

paragraphs: This paper examines occupational biases in GPT-2 as used directly from an accessible model library. Its focus is intersectional: it studies gender together with religion, sexuality, ethnicity, political affiliation, and continental name origin. The question is how combinations of these categories relate to the occupations generated by the model.

The researchers collect 396,000 sentence completions through a template-based pipeline and fit 262 logistic models to quantify occupational associations. They find that generated jobs are less varied and more stereotypical for women than for men, particularly when intersecting categories are considered. The statistical analysis also finds that interactions between categories matter, making separate analyses of individual categories insufficient to describe these observed associations.

For most occupations, the model reflects gender and ethnicity imbalances found in US labor data. Where predictions diverge from observed labor patterns, the authors also report movement toward gender parity. These findings raise a normative question about model behavior: whether generated associations should reproduce existing social distributions or help correct their inequalities.
neurips-2021-bias-out-of-the-box-an-empi.tldr: An analysis of GPT-2 completions finds occupational stereotypes shaped by intersecting social categories and raises questions about reproducing labor-market inequalities.

paragraphs: This paper models interactions between pairs of entities as events occurring in continuous time. Reciprocity is a central concern: an interaction in one direction can increase the tendency for a response. Mutually exciting Hawkes processes capture this behavior, but existing implementations often restrict how event rates change or require computationally expensive inference.

The authors develop three variants of nonparametric point-process models for continuous-time edges. Their intensity functions, which describe how likely events are to occur over time, are generated through sigmoidal Gaussian processes. This gives the models more flexibility than fixed parametric forms. A new edge-modeling construction also enables fast variational inference, addressing the computational burden associated with commonly used Markov chain Monte Carlo methods.

Evaluations on four real-world datasets demonstrate superior performance for the proposed models in the reported experiments. The contribution combines adaptable descriptions of interaction timing with a more efficient inference procedure. This matters because a flexible event model is more useful when its unknown quantities can also be estimated efficiently.
neurips-2021-continuous-time-edge-modell.tldr: Three flexible point-process models combine Gaussian-process event rates with fast variational inference for continuous-time interactions.

paragraphs: Neural recording systems face a bandwidth trade-off between observing more neurons and sampling them more frequently. This paper exploits relationships among neurons to recover activity from recordings where different variables are observed at different times. Its premise is that shared, low-dimensional population dynamics contain information that can help reconstruct missing samples.

The proposed training strategy, selective backpropagation through time, lets deep generative models learn those dynamics despite changing observation patterns. Applied to sequential autoencoders, it combines available measurements with learned latent dynamics to infer unobserved activity. The resulting super-resolution concerns both which neurons are represented and how finely their activity is resolved over time.

Experiments show more efficient and higher-fidelity characterization of electrophysiological and calcium-imaging data. Accurate inference at lower electrophysiological bandwidths suggests a route to power savings in implanted interfaces. In two-photon imaging, the method recovers high-frequency temporal structure and substantially outperforms the compared state of the art. Limited high-bandwidth pretraining followed by adaptation to sparse recordings can further improve performance.
neurips-2021-deep-inference-of-latent-dy.tldr: Selective backpropagation through time learns shared neural dynamics from changing observation patterns to reconstruct missing neuronal activity.

paragraphs: Many theoretical descriptions of neural-network training provide bounds on loss that can be rigorous yet loose. This paper instead derives the leading behavior of loss at large training times. Its setting is a wide network in the lazy training regime, where the analysis uses a linearized description of the network's evolution.

The main result gives a power law: loss behaves asymptotically like a constant multiplied by training time raised to a negative exponent. That exponent depends only on the data dimension, activation-function smoothness, and the class of functions being approximated. This connects the long-time rate of learning to structural properties of the problem and network, rather than describing it only through an upper bound.

The derivation uses spectral analysis of an integral operator governing training on expected loss. It does not require a particular data-distribution form such as a Gaussian. That broadens the distributions covered by the analysis, while the stated wide-network, lazy-training, and large-time conditions remain central to interpreting the result.
neurips-2021-explicit-loss-asymptotics-i.tldr: For wide networks in lazy training, the paper derives a long-time loss power law determined by dimension, activation smoothness, and target-function class.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning uses experience across tasks to learn how to adapt quickly to related new tasks. Sparse rewards make this difficult because useful feedback is rarely encountered. Existing methods may adapt to sparse-reward tasks while still depending on hand-designed dense rewards during meta-training, or on environments simple enough for random exploration to find rewards.

This paper introduces hindsight task relabelling for meta-reinforcement learning. It relabels experience during meta-training so that learning an adaptation strategy can itself proceed entirely with sparse rewards. The key contribution concerns the training of the learning strategy, addressing the stage where earlier approaches often required a richer reward signal than the actual task provides.

The authors evaluate the method on challenging sparse-reward environments that previously needed dense rewards during meta-training to solve. Their approach solves these environments with the true sparse reward function and achieves performance comparable to training with a proxy dense reward. The results demonstrate that experience relabelling can reduce dependence on manually shaped feedback in the tested meta-learning problems.
neurips-2021-hindsight-task-relabelling-.tldr: Hindsight task relabelling enables meta-reinforcement learning with sparse rewards throughout training, matching dense-reward training performance on the tested environments.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms must make decisions without knowing the environment in advance. This paper seeks algorithms that automatically benefit from favorable patterns while retaining guarantees when conditions are difficult. It measures performance through regret, which captures the cost of the algorithm's decisions relative to a comparison choice.

For combinatorial semi-bandits, the proposed algorithm has a hybrid guarantee with two components. A best-of-three-worlds result gives nearly optimal behavior in adversarial, stochastic, and adversarially corrupted stochastic environments. Additional data-dependent bounds reward easier loss sequences even when those sequences are far from stochastic. The relevant measures include the cumulative loss of optimal actions, total quadratic variation, and the path-length of the loss sequence.

The paper also establishes hybrid data-dependent guarantees for adversarial linear bandits. These include a first path-length regret bound that is tight up to logarithmic factors. Together, the results show how one algorithmic framework can retain broad protection while offering stronger guarantees when particular measurable properties of the environment are favorable.
neurips-2021-hybrid-regret-bounds-for-co.tldr: Hybrid regret guarantees let bandit algorithms exploit favorable loss patterns without prior knowledge while retaining protection across challenging environments.

paragraphs: This paper introduces iterative causal discovery, ICD, for learning causal graph structure when hidden confounders and selection bias may be present. Under the causal Markov and faithfulness assumptions, the algorithm recovers the equivalence class of the underlying causal graph. Its target therefore represents causal structures compatible with the available independence information.

ICD begins with every pair of nodes connected and repeatedly refines the graph through conditional-independence tests. It links the size of each conditioning set to its graph distance from the tested nodes, increasing this value across iterations. Earlier rounds use smaller conditioning sets, whose greater statistical power helps provide a stable graph for later refinement.

The algorithm is sound and complete under its stated assumptions, and the independence and causal relations established after each iteration are correct within that framework. This makes ICD an anytime method: intermediate iterations already supply valid deductions. Empirical comparisons show significantly fewer independence tests and more accurate recovered graphs than FCI, FCI+, and RFCI.
neurips-2021-iterative-causal-discovery-.tldr: ICD progressively refines causal graphs under stated assumptions, with valid intermediate deductions and fewer independence tests in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Attention in a graph neural network helps determine which node information receives emphasis as representations are propagated. This paper introduces Conjoint Attentions, which combine the node features available within a network layer with additional structural information. The aim is to make attention sensitive to useful graph organization beyond the current propagated features.

The structural inputs can include node-cluster embeddings and higher-order correlations learned outside the graph neural network. These signals participate in computing attention scores, making features judged significant by the combined criteria more likely to be propagated. The authors build Graph conjoint attention networks, or CATs, around these strategies so that learned representations incorporate the features selected through this broader attention mechanism.

The paper provides theoretical validation of CATs' discriminative capacity and evaluates them extensively on established benchmark datasets against state-of-the-art baselines. The reported performance supports the effectiveness of combining internal node features with external structural signals. Its contribution is a class of attention strategies together with network architectures that put those strategies into practice.
neurips-2021-learning-conjoint-attention.tldr: Conjoint Attentions combine propagated node features with additional graph structure to guide information flow in graph neural networks.

paragraphs: Large image datasets are costly to curate and raise concerns about inherited biases, privacy, and usage rights. This paper asks whether useful visual representations can be learned without real-image training datasets. It explores procedurally generated images produced by simple random processes as an alternative source of training material.

The researchers study several families of generators: statistical image models, randomly initialized deep generative models, and procedural graphics models. Their generated images train a visual representation learner using a contrastive loss. Comparing these sources allows the study to examine which properties of synthetic visual input matter, including whether the images need to look realistic to be useful.

The findings indicate that some structural properties of real data are important, but convincing realism is not required for good performance in the studied setting. Diversity also emerges as a key ingredient for learning good representations. The contribution is evidence about what generated training images need to provide, supporting procedural data as a potential alternative to collecting real photographs.
neurips-2021-learning-to-see-by-looking-.tldr: Visual representations can learn effectively from procedural noise when the generated images provide useful structure and diversity.

paragraphs: Running vision networks on microcontrollers is constrained by extremely limited memory. This paper identifies an imbalance in convolutional networks: their first few blocks consume roughly an order of magnitude more memory than later blocks. The proposed response is to process small spatial patches of feature maps, reducing how much intermediate information must be held at once.

Patch processing introduces its own cost because overlapping regions can require repeated computation. The authors reduce this overhead by moving receptive-field growth and computation toward later stages. Neural architecture search jointly chooses the network architecture and inference schedule, automating this difficult design problem and producing MCUNetV2.

Patch-based inference reduces peak memory for existing networks by four to eight times. With joint design, MCUNetV2 reaches 71.8% ImageNet accuracy on a microcontroller and exceeds 90% accuracy on visual wake words with 32 kB of SRAM. The authors also report improved Pascal VOC object detection. These results show how memory-aware execution and architecture design can enable vision tasks beyond classification on tiny devices.
neurips-2021-memory-efficient-patch-base.tldr: MCUNetV2 jointly designs networks and patch-based execution to reduce peak memory and enable stronger vision models on microcontrollers.

paragraphs: Object detection and instance segmentation models can favor classes that appear frequently in training data. This is especially problematic in long-tailed datasets, where many categories have relatively few examples. While existing solutions mostly change training through sampling or weighting, this paper investigates adjusting confidence scores after the model has made its predictions.

The proposed method, Normalized Calibration or NorCal, reweights each class's predicted scores using its training sample count. Two design choices are central: treating the background class separately and normalizing scores across classes for each proposed object region. Together, these choices address how class-frequency information enters the final competition among predicted categories.

On LVIS, NorCal improves nearly all evaluated baseline models. The gains extend beyond rare categories to common and frequent ones, showing that the reported benefits are not restricted to the least represented classes. Extensive analyses and ablations examine the method's mechanisms and design choices. The results establish post-processing calibration as an effective additional approach to long-tailed detection and segmentation.
neurips-2021-on-model-calibration-for-lo.tldr: NorCal adjusts detection and segmentation confidence scores using class frequency, improving nearly all tested LVIS baselines across frequency groups.

paragraphs: Distributed learning with a central server requires communication both from workers to the server and back again. Compressing these messages reduces communication demands, but compression also affects the learning process. This paper proposes MCM, an algorithm that compresses both directions while achieving the same convergence rate as algorithms that compress only worker-to-server messages.

Its key design choice is to preserve the central model while allowing downlink compression to perturb the models held by individual workers. Workers therefore compute gradients using these perturbed local models. The distinction matters because errors introduced during distribution remain in local copies instead of directly altering the global model being maintained by the server.

Proving convergence requires careful control of the local perturbations. MCM combines model compression with a memory mechanism to support that control. The analysis establishes the claimed convergence-rate improvement and opens possibilities for incorporating worker-dependent randomized models and partial participation. The contribution connects a specific model-preservation design with guarantees for communication-efficient distributed optimization.
neurips-2021-preserved-central-model-for.tldr: MCM preserves the central model while compressing both communication directions, matching the convergence rate of uplink-only compression.

paragraphs: Self-supervised visual learning often emphasizes making different augmented views of the same image agree. This paper shifts attention toward relationships between different images. Its framework, relational self-supervised learning or ReSSL, learns representations by using the pattern of similarities among instances as a training signal.

ReSSL represents those relationships with a sharpened distribution of pairwise similarities. That distribution is used to match feature embeddings across augmentations, encouraging consistency in how instances relate to one another. The authors argue that weak augmentation helps produce a more reliable relational signal. They also incorporate a momentum strategy to make the approach practically efficient.

The reported experiments show significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods in both performance and training efficiency. These findings support using relationships across examples as useful supervision beyond agreement between views of an individual example. The method's design also highlights that augmentation strength affects the reliability of the relational information being used to train the representation.
neurips-2021-ressl-relational-self-super.tldr: ReSSL learns visual representations by matching relationships among images, using weak augmentation to make those relationships more reliable.

paragraphs: An explanation of a model prediction can be unreliable if it changes unpredictably when the input is transformed. This paper addresses that problem by training a self-interpretable model with transformation-equivariant regularization. The goal is for geometric changes to an input to produce corresponding changes in its interpretation.

Equivariance gives explanation consistency a concrete training target: the interpretation should track the transformation applied to the data. Because the model is self-interpretable, its explanations are tied to its predictive mechanism. The authors aim to combine this faithfulness with robustness, so that a visually accessible explanation both reflects how the model predicts and behaves consistently under geometric transformations.

The paper reports that its model retains expressive capability comparable to state-of-the-art deep models on complex tasks while producing high-quality visual interpretations. Comparisons with related methods validate interpretation quality and consistency. These findings support the possibility of building explanatory structure into a powerful predictive model without the expressive-power sacrifice commonly associated with existing self-interpretable approaches.
neurips-2021-self-interpretable-model-wi.tldr: A self-interpretable model uses transformation-equivariant regularization to produce faithful, geometrically consistent explanations while retaining strong expressive capability.

paragraphs: Gradient descent ascent is a standard way to train competing objectives, but its behavior can be difficult to characterize. This paper studies hidden zero-sum games: players control inputs to smooth, possibly nonlinear functions whose outputs enter a convex-concave game. This underlying structure defines a target solution through the hidden game's von Neumann equilibrium.

The authors give conditions under which ordinary gradient descent ascent converges to that target, beyond merely reaching a local Nash equilibrium. Their results are non-local despite the non-convex, non-concave formulation. Under appropriate assumptions, they combine the Center-Stable Manifold Theorem with initialization-dependent Lyapunov functions to prove convergence from almost all initial conditions.

Strict convexity properties matter. Without them, the dynamics may fail to converge to any equilibrium. Standard regularization nevertheless permits a convergence proof for a slightly perturbed game. The framework therefore identifies both conditions supporting convergence and a way to recover a related guarantee when those properties are absent, with applications discussed from generative adversarial networks to evolutionary biology.
neurips-2021-solving-min-max-optimizatio.tldr: Hidden convex-concave structure yields conditional convergence guarantees for gradient descent ascent in certain non-convex, non-concave games.

paragraphs: A trained classifier may encounter images whose distribution differs from its training domains. This paper introduces the test-time template adjuster, T3A, to use incoming unlabeled data when making predictions under such shifts. It operates on the trained model's final linear classifier, providing a test-time mechanism for adjusting classification.

T3A constructs a pseudo-prototype representation for each class using online unlabeled examples together with information from the source-trained classifier. It then classifies each sample according to its distance from those prototypes. The procedure requires no backpropagation and modifies only the linear layer, giving negligible additional inference cost according to the authors. It also avoids the potential catastrophic failures associated with stochastic optimization during adaptation.

Experiments span PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and TerraIncognita and include convolutional, Transformer, and MLP-Mixer backbones. T3A consistently improves performance on unseen domains across the evaluated backbone choices and outperforms existing domain-generalization methods in these tests. The results support lightweight classifier adjustment as a useful way to exploit information available at deployment.
neurips-2021-test-time-classifier-adjust.tldr: T3A uses unlabeled test data to adjust class prototypes without backpropagation, improving unseen-domain classification across the evaluated models.

paragraphs: A human pose estimator trained on diverse data can still struggle with an unfamiliar person or environment. This paper personalizes a 2D pose estimator using a set of test images of one person, without requiring manual annotations. The aim is to exploit person-specific information available when the model is actually used.

Training combines supervised and self-supervised pose-estimation objectives. A Transformer learns a mapping between the keypoints produced by the self-supervised task and those associated with the supervised task. At test time, the model is fine-tuned through its self-supervised objective. The learned transformation then converts the updated self-supervised keypoints into an improved pose estimate.

This design connects an annotation-free adaptation signal to the supervised pose output through the Transformer mapping. The authors report significant improvements across multiple datasets after self-supervised personalization. Their findings show that a person's test images can provide useful adaptation information, allowing the estimator to respond to the individual case through a training objective that does not need new manual labels.
neurips-2021-test-time-personalization-w.tldr: A Transformer links self-supervised and supervised keypoints so a pose estimator can personalize itself from unlabeled images of a person.

paragraphs: Virtual try-on systems often depend on carefully paired training examples, making data collection restrictive and laborious. PASTA-GAN addresses garment transfer between people using unpaired training. Its central challenge is separating a garment's appearance from the spatial arrangement imposed by the person currently wearing it.

The model uses the source person's keypoints to divide a garment into normalized patches. This removes its original spatial arrangement while retaining texture and shape characteristics. It then reconstructs those patches into a warped garment that follows the target person's pose. Spatially adaptive residual blocks use the warped garment to guide the generator toward more realistic clothing details.

Comparisons with paired and unpaired approaches demonstrate superior results in the reported evaluations, including high-quality transfers across varied garments such as vests, shirts, and pants. The approach combines an explicit patch transformation with end-to-end image synthesis. Its significance lies in preserving garment appearance while adapting pose, supporting virtual try-on systems that can scale without the same paired-data collection requirements.
neurips-2021-towards-scalable-unpaired-v.tldr: PASTA-GAN transfers clothing between people using normalized garment patches and spatially guided generation, without paired training data.

paragraphs: Instance-based interpretation explains a model by examining the role of individual training examples. Such methods are well studied for supervised prediction, but their meaning is less clear in unsupervised learning. This paper investigates that question for variational autoencoders, a class of deep generative models, with a particular focus on influence functions.

The authors formally specify the counterfactual question that influence functions answer in this setting. Their theoretical analysis examines what these tools reveal about how training samples affect classical unsupervised learning methods. This step matters because an influence score needs a clear interpretation: identifying influential examples is useful only when the effect being measured is well defined.

The paper then introduces VAE-TracIn, a computationally efficient method with theoretical grounding for variational autoencoders. It evaluates the approach on several real-world datasets through quantitative and qualitative analyses. The contribution therefore combines a clearer conceptual account of training-example influence in unsupervised learning with a practical method for studying that influence in VAEs.
neurips-2021-understanding-instance-base.tldr: The paper clarifies training-example influence in unsupervised learning and introduces VAE-TracIn as an efficient, theoretically grounded interpretation method for VAEs.

paragraphs: Recovering both the locations and shapes of multiple objects from one image requires a representation useful for two different 3D tasks. This paper learns a regular grid of voxel features aligned with scene space. A feature-lifting operator maps information from the input image into that shared three-dimensional representation.

The CenterNet-3D detection head treats object detection as finding keypoints in 3D space. A separate coarse-to-fine module reconstructs shapes using coarse voxelization and a local PCA-SDF representation. Both tasks supervise the shared voxel features, encouraging them to preserve geometry and context. Their complementary training signals therefore benefit the representation used by each task.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness in both single-object and multiple-object settings. They report fine-detail reconstruction with inference two orders of magnitude faster than prior methods. The approach's significance is the combination of scene-aligned features, 3D detection, and efficient shape reconstruction within one system, allowing location and shape estimation to reinforce each other through shared learning.
neurips-2021-voxel-based-3d-detection-an.tldr: Shared 3D voxel features support joint object detection and detailed shape reconstruction from a single image, with substantially faster reported reconstruction inference.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often tie their message-passing structure directly to the input graph. This can restrict expressivity, long-range interaction, and the treatment of higher-order structures. This paper develops CW Networks by moving message passing onto regular cell complexes, mathematical structures that flexibly include graphs and simplicial complexes.

Different ways of lifting a graph into a cell complex produce different hierarchical message-passing procedures. The authors establish that the resulting methods are strictly more expressive than the Weisfeiler-Lehman test and at least as powerful as the 3-WL test. The architecture also provides principled handling of higher-order signals and compresses distances between nodes, addressing several limitations of ordinary graph-based computation.

For molecular problems, the paper examines a lifting scheme based on rings and reports state-of-the-art results across multiple molecular datasets. The theoretical and empirical contributions complement each other: cell complexes provide a broader representational framework, while the molecular experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of one concrete way to use that flexibility.
neurips-2021-weisfeiler-and-lehman-go-ce.tldr: CW Networks perform hierarchical message passing on cell complexes, gaining stronger expressivity and achieving leading results on molecular datasets.

paragraphs: Early-exit neural networks attach classifiers to intermediate layers so that easy inputs can receive a prediction before the full network runs. This reduces average inference time. However, when an intermediate classifier does not return an answer, its prediction is typically discarded even though the computation needed to produce it has already been performed.

Zero Time Waste, or ZTW, makes those earlier predictions available to later internal classifiers. It adds direct connections between classifiers and combines previous outputs in an ensemble-like manner. This allows subsequent decisions to reuse work done along the way, making the sequence of intermediate classifiers a source of accumulated predictive information.

Across experiments involving several datasets and architectures, ZTW achieves a significantly better accuracy-versus-inference-time trade-off than the compared recent early-exit methods. The result supports treating intermediate predictions as reusable evidence throughout inference. For applications balancing response time and prediction quality, the reported improvement means the early-exit design can make more effective use of computation already spent on an input.
neurips-2021-zero-time-waste-recycling-p.tldr: ZTW reuses earlier internal predictions in early-exit networks, improving the reported trade-off between accuracy and inference time.
